paragraphs.heading: Finding the size of a set
paragraphs.text: Counting means working out how many elements a finite set holds, in other words, its size. The traditional way keeps a counter, spoken aloud or kept in your head, and raises it by one for each element in turn. Each element gets marked or moved aside so it is never visited twice, and when nothing unmarked is left, the counter gives the total, provided it read one after the first object. Counting does not always go up in ones: people count money, count by twos (2, 4, 6, ...) or count by fives. A related idea, enumeration, gives each element of a finite or infinite set its own number so that it can be told apart from the rest.

paragraphs.heading: An ancient skill
paragraphs.text: Archaeological evidence suggests people have been counting for at least 50,000 years. Notched bones from the Border Caves in South Africa may point to counting as early as 44,000 BCE. Ancient cultures mostly counted to keep track of social and economic facts, such as how many people belonged to a group, how many prey animals there were, what property someone held, or what debts were owed. Counting in turn led to mathematical notation, numeral systems and writing.

paragraphs.heading: Ways of keeping count
paragraphs.text: Verbal counting means saying the numbers in order, out loud or silently, usually in base 10. It suits things that are in front of you right now, because an interrupted count has to pick up where it stopped, and that number must be remembered or written down. For a small set, especially one counted over time, tally marks work well: make one mark per item, then count the marks at the end. Fingers are handy for small numbers, and older methods used the three bones in each of four fingers to reach twelve. With finger binary you can count as high as 1023 = 2¹⁰ − 1, and tools such as tally counters and abacuses help too.

paragraphs.heading: Inclusive and exclusive counting
paragraphs.text: Inclusive and exclusive counting are two different methods. Inclusive counting begins with the start of the starting point and runs to the end of the last point. Exclusive counting counts at the end of each interval, so the starting point is left out. For the same set, the inclusive count always comes out one higher than the exclusive count.

paragraphs.heading: Calendars, words and music
paragraphs.text: Inclusive counting often turns up with time in Roman calendars and the Romance languages. Counted inclusively from a Sunday, that Sunday is day 1 and the next Sunday is the eighth day; in English, which counts exclusively, Monday is day 1 and the following Monday is day eight. For example, the French word for a fortnight, quinzaine, means fifteen days, and Spanish and Portuguese have similar words, quincena and quinzena. East Asian age reckoning works in a similar way, treating a newborn as 1. Music does too: one note up is a second, two notes up is a third, and seven notes up is an octave.

paragraphs.heading: Learning to count
paragraphs.text: In most cultures, learning to count is an important step in a child's development. From the age of two, children pick up the number words in order, first a short run and then longer and longer ones. At first they may say "one, two, three" without really knowing what each word means. Learning to count takes more than memorising the list: children must learn that each object is paired with just one number word, which is called one-to-one correspondence. In parts of Amazonia and the Australian Outback, some cultures have no counting at all, and no number words in their languages.
